item.title: Moon Journey ha comentado: Fun fact, a radio call from the Moon took a bit over a second to reach Houston. Voyager's now takes a whole day.
item.description: Help us celebrate a historic milestone for Voyager 1. Next week, our record-setting spacecraft will reach the "one light-day" mark—16 billion miles from... Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Water molecules turn out to be secret messengers for magnetism
item.description: Water is not usually thought of as a magnetic material. But a new study led by researchers at Tohoku University's Institute of Multidisciplinary Research for Advanced Materials, in collaboration with National Taipei University of Technology (Taipei Tech), has found that tiny shifts in the orientation of water molecules can flip on magnetic partnerships between metal ions that are not even directly bonded to each other. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Jinkx Monsoon and BenDeLaCreme on Taking Their Holiday Show on the Road and Paying Tribute to ‘Queer Icons’ Tim Curry and Dolly Parton
item.description: Yes, there are the Rockettes at Radio City Music Hall, but actors, writers, comedians and drag queens Jinkx Monsoon and BenDelaCreme are back to slay with one of the greatest and funniest winter shows — The Jinkx and Dela Holiday Show! This year, Monsoon and Dela celebrate their ninth year of taking the show on […] Fuente: Variety.
item.dc:creator: Jazztangcay

item.title: Harnessing laser nuisance achieves record resolution for atomic measurements
item.description: A shoebox-sized color detection device could enable precise measurements at record resolution, according to new research led by Adelaide University. An international team exploited an integrating sphere—a highly reflective hollow cavity that causes light to bounce around inside many times before exiting—to demonstrate a device that can measure the color (wavelength) composition of light with extreme precision at a resolution of just 6 femtometers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Prison data analysis finds choosing lowest reoffending risk scores preserves overall accuracy
item.description: Whether an individual reoffends after their release from prison or is successfully rehabilitated depends on several factors. When assessing the risk of recidivism, all of these are taken into account—both by human experts and by machine learning models. If several equally reliable computational models produce different risk ratings, the lowest value should be used for the individual concerned, suggest Ashwin Singh (TU Wien) and Carlos Castillo (ICREA/Universitat Pompeu Fabra). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sexual violence can hide in plain sight at music festivals, according to new study
item.description: The pressure to maintain an atmosphere of fun and escapism can make it harder for festival organizations to acknowledge and respond to harm, while frontline workers are left dealing with its consequences, a new study finds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Seafloor clay reveals past dramatic ice loss in West Antarctica
item.description: Scientists have discovered the best evidence yet to show that West Antarctica's most vulnerable ice streams—including its giant Thwaites Glacier—repeatedly collapsed and retreated far inland during natural warm periods of the last 800,000 years. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Swordfish may be using deep dives to navigate the open ocean
item.description: Swordfish spend much of their time hunting prey about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface in the ocean twilight zone, but occasionally, they reach depths of more than 1,000 meters (3,280 feet). Now, scientists from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) are investigating what may be behind these extreme dives. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI-generated molecular fingerprints help identify existing compounds with therapeutic potential
item.description: Health care researchers have long sought to harness the power of computing to design molecules that bind to specific receptors and can be used as targeted treatments for diseases. Even with the increasing sophistication of artificial intelligence, however, this technological promise has yet to be realized. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Detailed 3D view of babesiosis parasite's ribosome could guide development of targeted treatments
item.description: A new study has revealed a three-dimensional, near-atomic-resolution view of the ribosome from Babesia divergens, one of several Babesia species known to infect humans and cause babesiosis. The structural insights from this close-up view could help researchers identify parasite-specific features that may be exploited for future drug development. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Germany's Isar Aerospace eyes overtaking Elon Musk's SpaceX
item.description: The head of Germany's Isar Aerospace voiced hope Tuesday that the company could one day overtake Elon Musk's SpaceX to become the world's premier space launch company. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: By carefully arranging molecules, scientists can control how a material responds to light, heat and physical force
item.description: University of Missouri researchers have created a single solid material that responds differently depending on what it's exposed to. Shine light on it, and it changes from yellow to white, an indication of a chemical reaction. Heat it, and it undergoes a different chemical reaction. Scratch the surface, and it flashes blue. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Influencers are supposed to influence us—so why are they asking us what they should do?
item.description: An influencer posts a photograph of two designer handbags and asks her followers which one she should buy. Another wants recommendations for restaurants in a new city she is visiting. Someone else asks which beauty dupes are actually worth trying. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Coral colony the size of three MCGs thriving off remote Australian island
item.description: An enormous rose coral colony, one of the largest ever recorded, is mapped by a team of researchers off the Cocos (Keeling) Islands. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Amy Rossbach

item.title: How the cosmic environment depletes galaxies of their gas
item.description: An international team of researchers, led by Jonathan Freundlich (University of Strasbourg, Astronomical Observatory), has revealed how a dense cosmic environment depletes galaxies of their gas. By mapping the molecular gas in a galaxy group located 7 billion light-years away, they found that the galaxies in this group harbor, on average, gas reservoirs reduced by more than half compared to similar isolated galaxies. The results of this study are published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Antarctic water analysis reveals unexpected stability in dissolved organic carbon
item.description: Researchers have analyzed water samples collected during two expeditions aboard the research icebreaker Polarstern to investigate how life and changing conditions on the Antarctic continental shelf affect carbon carried into the deep ocean. Published in Nature Communications, the study reveals a surprising finding: Despite intense biological activity and major changes in the water masses, the amount and make-up of dissolved organic matter remain almost unchanged. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rusia lanzó un estudio con 7.000 primates para cumplir los sueños de "vida eterna" de Vladimir Putin
item.description: Uno de los centros de investigación estatal más importantes del país explora formas de alargar la esperanza de vida saludable. Este asunto es una prioridad para el Kremlin. El Estado destina fondos millonarios a trabajos de genética, medicina nuclear y otras tecnologías asociadas a la salud. Fuente: Clarín - Mundo.
item.dc:creator: Clarin.com - Home

item.title: When a Walmart closes, what happens to nearby stores?
item.description: Shoppers often greet the closure of a Walmart with dismay, while competitors find cause to celebrate. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover new way to control magnetic waves for future quantum technologies
item.description: Researchers at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Ames National Laboratory have discovered a way to control the handedness of magnons, tiny magnetic waves that can carry information through materials. By changing the material's magnetic state with an external magnetic field, they were able to switch magnon behavior, a finding with potential applications in quantum information and quantum computing technologies. Their findings are published in Physical Review Letters. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Classical–quantum light interactions could make complex quantum behavior easier to simulate
item.description: An international collaboration demonstrates that classical nonlinear dynamics can drive single- and two-photon states to thermalize, opening new avenues for simulating complex quantum many-body systems within accessible optical architectures. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI use is now universal in higher education. Why are universities failing to adapt?
item.description: Artificial intelligence use among university students is now near-universal in many countries. Yet, as of a year ago, fewer than one in five universities in a 90-country UNESCO survey had a formal AI policy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Earth's 'core carbon' may have come from the far reaches of the solar system
item.description: A new study suggests that most of Earth's carbon originated in the outer solar system and didn't arrive here until the late stages of planetary development. The study, led by researchers at Yale and Columbia, is based upon an analysis of magma droplets called "melt inclusions" from historic volcano eruptions in Hawaii, including the Keanakākoʻi eruptions from 1500 to 1840 and the Kīlauea Iki eruption in 1959. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Poles of bacteria imaged in fine detail for the first time
item.description: The poles, or ends, of rod-shaped bacteria have been imaged at molecular resolution for the first time in a new study led by UCL (University College London) researchers. The study, published in the journal Nature Communications, used a new technique to keep live bacteria in place so the cells could be imaged without wriggling away. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New approach boosts plastic-eating enzyme's activity nearly tenfold
item.description: Researchers from King's College London and Rutgers University in New Jersey created a modified enzyme (a protein that speeds up chemical reactions) that breaks down polyethylene terephthalate (PET) plastic 10 times quicker, using 10 times less enzyme. They accomplished this just by changing the liquid it works in and making small changes to the enzyme's structure. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Financial institutions tout sustainability while still funding high-carbon projects, review finds
item.description: A review published in the International Journal of Managerial and Financial Accounting on the subject of greenwashing in financial services has found that financial institutions often claim environmental responsibility while continuing to finance high-carbon projects. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Protein-building RNA molecules reveal possible remnants of an ancestral genetic code
item.description: The genetic code determines the correspondence between genetic instructions and amino acids—the building blocks that form proteins. How this correspondence arose is one of the major open questions in evolutionary biology. A study led by Dr. Lluís Ribas de Pouplana, ICREA researcher at IRB Barcelona, and Dr. Paul Schimmel, with the participation of researchers from MIT and Scripps Research, has identified conserved signals in transfer RNAs that could help reconstruct the early stages of this system. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Webb's controversial 'little red dots' may finally have an explanation
item.description: Astronomers may have solved one of the biggest mysteries uncovered by NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), using sophisticated simulations to show that enigmatic objects known as "little red dots" (LRDs) are likely the birthplaces of the first supermassive black holes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Protein tails help shape mosquito cell-to-cell channels
item.description: Cells share small molecules with their neighbors through tiny tunnels made of proteins arranged in a ring. Research at Nagoya University suggests that the tails of the proteins must link up to form an inner ring for the tunnel to become evenly round—a previously unknown step in how these cell-to-cell connections are built. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Two new howler monkey species discovered in the Amazon after 85 years
item.description: Genetic research has uncovered two previously unknown species of howler monkey living in the Amazon rainforest, confirming the world's largest tropical forest is more biodiverse than scientists thought. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Lifesavers to trial AI tool to detect rip currents
item.description: UNSW researchers say the tool can pick out a rip in a photograph of a beach, and hope it can be used to help save lives. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Declan Bowring

item.title: Gravitational waves hint at black holes born from failed supernovae
item.description: When the most massive stars in the universe die, they often detonate in fiery supernovae, dramatically blasting most of their matter into space. The remaining stellar cores collapse into neutron stars and, sometimes, black holes. However, theories suggest that some massive stars might die without a bang, instead directly collapsing inward to become neutron stars or black holes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: When the definition of sexual consent gets stretched
item.description: Men in treatment for domestic violence have an elastic view of what constitutes consent in their partner, an UdeM study has found. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Repeatable laser measurements reveal 'forbidden' vibrations in single molecules without destroying them
item.description: The possibility of controlling "forbidden" excitations of vibrations in molecules could form the basis of extremely accurate clocks, quantum bits and precise tests of the fundamental laws of physics. Researchers at the University of Basel have now identified and controlled such "forbidden" transitions in single isolated nitrogen molecules without destroying them. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Help us celebrate a historic milestone for Voyager 1.... Ver más
item.description: Help us celebrate a historic milestone for Voyager 1.... Ver más Fun fact, a radio call from the Moon took a bit over a second to reach Houston. Voyager's now takes a whole day. Ver más comentarios Moon Journey Fuente: NASA.

item.title: NASA Invites Media, Public to Join Voyager 1 One-Light Day Activities
item.description: Launched nearly 50 years ago in 1977, NASA’s Voyager 1 on Wednesday, Nov. 18 will have traveled one light-day from Earth, which is more than 16 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object, and any light from Earth would take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft. NASA will highlight […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Gerelle Q. Dodson

item.title: NASA to Welcome Expedition 74 Astronauts Home at Space Center Houston
item.description: NASA will welcome home the Expedition 74 crew during a public event at Space Center Houston following their return from a long-duration mission aboard the International Space Station. NASA astronauts Jessica Meir, Jack Hathaway, and Chris Williams; ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Sophie Adenot; and Roscosmos cosmonauts Sergey Kud‑Sverchkov and Sergei Mikaev will share mission […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Wendy K. Avedisian

item.title: Janine Mulberry ha comentado: It was an awesome show!🔥
item.description: We had a great time at MAX POWER — and made a lot of news! We're recruiting a new class of astronauts, making major advancements on the Moon Base, and... Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Janine Mulberry ha comentado: It was an awesome show!🔥
item.description: We had a great time at MAX POWER — and made a lot of news! We're recruiting a new class of astronauts, making major advancements on the Moon Base, and... Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Tiny solar whirlpools may hold the secret to the sun's blistering corona
item.description: For the second time in a few weeks, we're writing about research into the temperature gap between the sun's surface and its corona. More and more data from various missions continue to feed this wave of discovery. A new paper by Katariina Nykyri of Embry-Riddle, recently published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, adds to this growing body of work. She argues that millions of tiny whirlpools scattered across the sun's surface could be the energetic engine driving that temperature difference. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Simulated moon dust turned into LEGO-like blocks for settlements
item.description: Permanent structures on the moon could start with something already there: lunar dust. New research from the University of Arkansas shows that pure regolith, the loose material that covers the moon, could be 3D-printed into LEGO-like bricks. Using it for construction could reduce what NASA needs to send from Earth as it works toward future lunar settlements. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: COP31 electric power target sparks row over cutting fossil fuel use
item.description: While hosts Türkiye push for countries to increase electrification of global energy use, Australia is pushing for more households to be fitted with solar panels. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Laura Tingle

item.title: What a 99-million-year-old feather is telling us about the evolution of flight
item.description: Long before birds took to the skies, dinosaurs were already sporting feathers. But exactly how they evolved into the sophisticated structures that allow birds to fly remains something of a mystery. Now, the discovery of the longest feather ever found preserved in amber is providing some new clues. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 7,000-year-old scrap of goat leather from a Spanish burial cave contains DNA
item.description: Researchers studied a 7,000-year-old goat leather fragment from Cueva de los Murciélagos in southern Spain. The specimen offers valuable genetic information about ancient goats and their domestication. Analysis revealed the goat's DNA connected to modern breeds, indicating genetic continuity over millennia. Evidence suggests humans may have processed the leather, leaving traces of their DNA behind. This research improves understanding of livestock management in Early Neolithic communities. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Cool adaptations: How fish survive in the Antarctic Ocean
item.description: With water temperatures as low as -1.9°C (28.6°F), the Southern Ocean is a place of extreme living conditions. A new study led by Senckenberg researchers shows how fish have adapted to Antarctic temperatures. The researchers used the Antarctic spiny plunderfish (Harpagifer antarcticus) as a model organism and, for the first time, analyzed the maternal and paternal copies of its genome separately. This allowed them to uncover mechanisms that contribute to this group of fishes' adaptation to extreme cold. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Q&A: Exploring generative AI's impact on student thinking during programming and debugging
item.description: The doctoral dissertation of Yazid Albadarin, MSc, entitled "Capturing the impact of generative AI on higher-order thinking, creativity, and cognitive dynamics during debugging" will be examined at the Faculty of Science, Forestry and Technology, Joensuu campus. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: At 1,700 metres beneath the Atlantic, mussels live in darkness and follow the tides
item.description: A groundbreaking study from the University of Vienna found that deep-sea mussels have an intricate 24-hour biological clock. These remarkable creatures thrive around hydrothermal vents, in pitch-black environments shaped by tidal forces. By culturing their cells, researchers opened doors for new biological investigations. Key clock genes crucial for controlling these rhythms were uncovered, shedding light on the intricate life systems thriving in the deep ocean's depths. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Antikythera Mechanism showcases ingenuity of Greek engineers with this ancient computing marvel
item.description: The Antikythera Mechanism stands as an extraordinary artifact from ancient Greece, ingeniously crafted for studying celestial movements and forecasting astronomical events. Dating back approximately 2,100 years, it showcases remarkable engineering through its sophisticated gears. Found in 1900 by sponge divers off the coast of Antikythera, this mechanism highlights the advanced scientific knowledge of the Greeks and continues to intrigue scholars by uncovering previously lost insights into technology and astronomy. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Lifestyle Desk

item.title: Laser-driven magnetic state defies equilibrium rules
item.description: Researchers at the Department of Energy's (DOE's) Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) and their collaborators used lasers and neutrons to observe a long-lived quantum state in a magnetic material, opening a new way to study materials systems driven far from their equilibrium. Manipulation of quantum magnets is important for advancing quantum information science and could reduce loss of transported information, improve memory devices and benefit other quantum technologies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Severe ocean risks threaten food prices, pensions and global economic resilience
item.description: Ocean risks are already severe and worsening, with the potential to become catastrophic without a change of course, according to a new report from the Institute and Faculty of Actuaries (IFoA), the University of Exeter and The Ocean Race. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: LHC collaboration presents first result in the hunt for 'quirks'
item.description: An international collaboration of physicists has presented its first results in its search for hypothetical particles that could help to explain the vast disparity between the strength of gravity and the three fundamental forces described by the Standard Model. Following three years of data collection at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC)'s FASER experiment, the FASER Collaboration found no evidence for these heavy, slow-moving "quirks." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Crystal boundaries help hydrogen sensors work in hot, humid air
item.description: Hydrogen could play an important role in cleaner energy systems, but even small leaks can create safety risks. Reliable sensors are therefore essential wherever hydrogen is produced, stored, transported or used. A persistent problem is humidity: water molecules can cover the active surfaces of hydrogen detectors and prevent them from responding accurately, particularly in hot, moisture-rich environments. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researcher uses AI to predict probabilities for chemical processes
item.description: Quantum chemistry can be used to calculate the probabilities of which chemical processes will occur. This involves a great deal of programming work. Dr. Michael F. Peintinger from the Mulliken Center for Theoretical Chemistry at the University of Bonn has investigated what happens when artificial intelligence is used for this purpose. His work is published in the Journal of Computational Chemistry. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why the current strategy to manage mule deer populations may not be working
item.description: Following a surge of interest in deer hunting beginning in the '80s and '90s, strategies to manage deer populations evolved to increase the proportion of mature male deer. While the increase in male abundance has perhaps made for better hunting conditions, the overall mule deer population in western North America has continued to decline. New BYU research appears to have figured out at least one potential reason why. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Finland's white-tailed eagle success story: What long-term data reveal about recovery
item.description: The white-tailed eagle (Haliaeetus albicilla) was once a rare species in Europe due to persecution and pollution. Thanks to legal protection and cleaner environments, many populations have been increasing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: X-ray observations uncover possible jet warning signs in black hole systems
item.description: Black hole jet ejections are powerful outbursts of high-energy photons and particles that provide insights into extreme astrophysical processes. However, predicting when they will occur remains difficult. In a study, researchers from Japan analyzed observations of four black hole binary systems, identifying decreases in the accretion disk's inner radius and changes in emitted X-ray variability as possible predictors for jet ejection. Their findings could help astronomers forecast these phenomena more accurately and coordinate timely observations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: One space station company sues another for copying its work
item.description: "NASA advised that Vast’s submission in some locations substituted 'the PAM Provider' for Axiom" Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Eric Berger

item.title: NASA Scientists Show How Gravitational Waves Can Reveal New Worlds
item.description: The LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) observatory, now in development, will detect gravitational waves, the tiny ripples in space-time caused by orbiting masses. Now two studies led by NASA astrophysicists show in new detail how LISA could reveal a new and unique population of exoplanets — worlds beyond our solar system — throughout our galaxy. […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Tiny nutrient, big mystery: Key gene reveals how cereal crops transport nickel
item.description: Nickel plays an important physiological role in plants, but how it is transported over long distances from stems and leaves to grains was poorly understood for more than 50 years. Now researchers have identified a key transporter gene, ZmNAET1, that controls nickel accumulation in cereal grains. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Changing magnetic dimensionality boosts spin-wave frequency in Cr₂₋δTe₂
item.description: Magnons are quasiparticles that represent quantized spin waves in magnetic materials. They can carry information without moving electric charge, making them promising for future information technologies that could use less energy than conventional electronics. The frequency, stability and propagation distance of these waves are all important for their potential applications. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Molecular structures reveal how a bacteriophage protein inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis
item.description: Drug-resistant bacteria are becoming more common worldwide, posing a major public health challenge. Addressing this problem requires finding new ways to eliminate bacteria, which in turn requires analyzing essential cellular processes that could serve as targets for future antibiotics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Neighborhood ties and social connections are linked to high recycling participation
item.description: Waste separation and recycling are essential to achieving a circular economy and sustainable resource management; however, the long-term success of well-established recycling systems depends on the continued participation of local residents. This study examined how social capital, defined as social relationships characterized by trust, reciprocity and mutual support, is associated with waste separation behavior. The research is published in the Journal of Material Cycles and Waste Management. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ice Age camp reveals hunter-gatherers reached Italy thousands of years earlier than previously thought
item.description: A fresh excavation of the eastern deposit at Riparo Mochi, a rock shelter near today's French–Italian border, has pushed back the timeline for when Ice Age hunter-gatherers from Spain first entered Italy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How cells pull together: Theoretical study reveals a hidden source of attraction
item.description: Imagine two people standing on a stretchy sheet. When one pulls, the other feels the fabric move and responds with a pull of their own. Each adjustment changes what the other feels. Something similar happens between living cells. They tug on the material around them, sense the stretching caused by their neighbors and adjust their own forces. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Most university students now use AI, but that doesn't mean they like it
item.description: The university experience has changed drastically since artificial intelligence (AI) became widely available four years ago. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Repeat thieves without kleptomania struggle to adapt to rewards in decision-making test
item.description: Theft is almost universally considered an exploitative behavior. The conventional view underlying judicial systems is that the act of taking resources from others without offering compensation stems from moral and personal failings. As a result, these systems rely on the assumption that the threat or imposition of punishment will motivate criminal offenders to adjust their future behavior. Yet the outcome is not always success. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Team designs molecules that efficiently generate orange-to-red light for OLED displays
item.description: Most of us spend much of our day staring at organic light-emitting diodes, or OLEDs, which convert electricity into light to produce the colorful displays on smartphones, computer monitors and televisions. Although metal-free light-emitting materials that produce all colors are in demand, it has been difficult to make ones that efficiently emit orange-to-red light. Now, researchers led by the University of Osaka have shown that such materials do not need to be held in a rigid shape to work well: flexible molecules that can change shape can also emit orange-to-red light. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: CHAPEA Crew Leaves a Mark
item.description: The Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) Mission 2 crew arranged photos around a boot print in the simulated Martian sand outside their habitat on Aug. 31, 2026. The crew recently exited their habitat on Saturday, Oct. 31, after 378 days of isolation in a facility at the agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. Health […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: HQ Web Team

item.title: Study investigates what drivers would pay for 'salmon-safe' tires
item.description: The average person might be willing to pay a 10% premium for vehicle tires labeled as "salmon safe," according to a new study led by Washington State University. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A catalyst that protects itself while producing hydrogen
item.description: Cobalt phosphide (CoP) is a promising alternative to platinum for producing hydrogen from water. However, scientists have struggled to explain why it performs so well. Computer models have suggested that CoP should become unstable under the conditions used to produce hydrogen, yet experiments show that it remains active and durable in acidic, neutral and alkaline environments. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Las emisiones de combustibles fósiles caerán por primera vez desde la pandemia de covid, según un estudio
item.description: Las emisiones globales de combustibles fósiles podrían disminuir un 0,4% en 2026, por primera vez desde la pandemia de covid, impulsadas por la expansión de las energías renovables y el impacto de la guerra en Irán sobre los precios del petróleo. Así lo señalaron este martes investigadores del informe Global Carbon Budget, que advirtieron que el descenso podría ser temporal. Fuente: France 24 - Español.
item.dc:creator: France 24

item.title: Simulations cast doubt on unusual asteroid's 'dark comet' status
item.description: In 2031, Japan's Hayabusa2 spacecraft will arrive at the near-Earth asteroid 1998 KY26: a tiny body that is accelerating in a way that astronomers have struggled to explain. Some studies have suggested that the asteroid is pushed along by water escaping from it as gas, making it an as-yet theoretical "dark comet." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new role for chlorine: Uncovering anion redox in solid-state battery cathodes
item.description: As demand grows for safer and more capable rechargeable batteries, scientists are looking beyond the familiar metal-centered chemistry of conventional cathodes. A promising route is to draw additional charge from anions—the negatively charged atoms in a material—rather than relying on transition metals alone. Oxygen and sulfur have attracted substantial attention in this area. Whether chlorine can play a comparable role in chloride-based battery cathodes has been less clear. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists release large-scale in situ cryo-ET resource for mouse sperm ultrastructure
item.description: The scale, quality and regional coverage of public cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) data resources have been insufficient, severely limiting data reuse, cross-regional comparisons and the development of automated analysis methods. A new resource aims to help fill that gap, providing 1,413 reconstructed tomograms and associated data from wild-type C57BL/6J mouse sperm. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: World's most sensitive lab-based axion search presents its first results
item.description: Physicists at the ALPS II collaboration have reported the first results from the Any-Light-Particle-Search (ALPS) II experiment: the most sensitive instrument of its kind in the search for hypothetical "axions." Headed by Axel Lindner at the DESY Research Centre in Germany, the collaboration found no evidence for axions in this initial campaign, but its results offer valuable guidance for future runs: tightening the search for one of the most promising candidates for dark matter. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Data link trial: Chinese team finds hollow-core fibre cuts lag 30% across 1,000km
item.description: Light travels through conventional optical fibres at about 200,000km per second – about two-thirds the speed it travels in a vacuum – because the signals are passing through solid glass. When vast amounts of data are exchanged between computing centres hundreds or thousands of kilometres apart, this difference amounts to a substantial delay. Now, Chinese researchers have unveiled optical fibre that replaces the solid glass core with air, cutting the data transmission delay by about 30 per cent... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Chao Kong

item.title: Paraguay: sigue el misterio de la bóveda escondida detrás de una pared falsa en la mansión de Santiago Peña y no descartan detonarla
item.description: En allanamientos por la caída del Ueno Bank, la Fiscalía busca ingresar a un recinto oculto, protegido por un sofisticado sistema de seguridad. Para abrir la compuerta blindada, los investigadores evalúan varias medidas. Nadie sabe qué hay en el lugar. Fuente: Clarín - Mundo.
item.dc:creator: Clarin.com - Home

item.title: Egyptian cats meant for the gods led harsh lives, extensive museum collection reveals
item.description: More than 2,000 years ago, Egyptians offered cats to the gods. Now, a new study published in the Journal of Archaeological Science suggests that even cats destined for the gods did not necessarily live pampered lives. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Student team develops innovative 'Trojan horse' in the fight against the Asian hornet
item.description: An interdisciplinary team of students from the Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB) is taking part in iGEM, the international synthetic biology competition in Paris (Nov. 13–16), this fall. Using a clever combination of artificial intelligence, a mechanical trap and protein nanofibers, they are presenting a targeted method to efficiently control populations of the Asian hornet. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Digging up the past can change the ground beneath it
item.description: Archaeological excavation uncovers the past but also changes the landscape that has preserved sites for centuries or millennia. These changes influence water flow, soil erosion and the stability of exposed remains. Researchers from Istanbul Technical University and the U.S. have shown how computer models can assist archaeologists in understanding and planning for these effects, especially regarding erosion risks. Using an Early Bronze Age settlement in Türkiye as a case study, they reconstructed the landscape before and after excavation. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: In 2026, the world emitted 42.2 billion tonne of heat-trapping carbon dioxide from the burning of fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas. It's a 0.4% decrease from last year, according to the scientists of the Global Carbon Project Publicado también por: The Hindu - International. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Global fossil fuel emissions are expected to fall by 0.4 percent in 2026 for first time since the Covid pandemic, driven by the expansion of renewable energy and the oil price shock linked to the Iran war, researchers said Tuesday, who warned the decline may be short-lived. Fuente: France 24 - English.

item.title: Math anxiety may be stopping students from learning useful AI and data skills
item.description: Artificial intelligence is increasingly becoming part of everyday life and work. AI can generate information, summarize evidence and perform calculations. However, it does not remove the need for critical thinking and conceptual understanding. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Light-pulse pairs reveal the femtosecond decay of an inner-shell hole in xenon atoms
item.description: Researchers at the UVSOR Synchrotron Facility (Institute for Molecular Science, Japan) and partner institutions have observed the decay of a xenon 4d core hole, an inner-shell vacancy, directly in the time domain. They used pairs of phase-coherent extreme ultraviolet pulses from a synchrotron to make the photoelectron wave packets they released interfere. The contrast of the interference fringes decreased over a few femtoseconds as the delay between the pulses increased. A model using literature core-hole lifetimes of about 6 femtoseconds reproduced this rapid decay of the fringe contrast… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI-assisted atomic models reveal how protective shells regulate aluminum nanoparticle oxidation
item.description: Building an accurate model of how atoms interact is a complicated process. Researchers must choose new calculations, test successive models and track the mechanisms behind each interaction. But a newly developed AI agent called MLP Copilot has made this process much easier by bridging computational tools and scientific evidence with human supervision. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain
item.description: A surprising discovery suggests that some early signs of Alzheimer’s disease may begin outside the brain. Using miniature laboratory systems made from human cells, scientists found that genetic mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s can disrupt nerve-to-muscle connections without any involvement from the brain or spinal cord. This could help explain why some patients experience changes in balance, walking, and coordination long before memory problems develop. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Barium titanate's optical properties emerge more clearly after decades of widely varying measurements
item.description: A KAIST-led research team has characterized how light propagates through and is absorbed by barium titanate (BTO), a promising material for next-generation optical communication devices. By clarifying optical properties that had been difficult to determine because of the material's complex internal structure, the study provides a foundation for designing these devices. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Electrical technique concentrates milk without using heat, challenging traditional preservation methods
item.description: Dehydrating milk to turn it into powder is, today, an energy-intensive process that subjects the product to high temperatures. Powdered milk is widely used by the food industry and allows the product to be stored and transported in a stable condition for long periods of time without the need for refrigeration. While industrial methods are effective, they have high energy costs and can alter heat-sensitive components, such as whey proteins, enzymes or vitamins. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Global carbon emissions from fossil fuels are projected to decrease by 0.4% in 2026—driven by expansion of solar and wind power and the Iran conflict—according to new research by the Global Carbon Project. The 2026 edition (the 21st annual report) is published in the journal Earth System Science Data. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: You're walking through the farmers market with a screaming toddler tucked under your arm football style. You're tired, you're leaving without the produce you came for and you're embarrassed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: After 40 years, CERN finds evidence of a one-in-10-billion particle decay
item.description: CERN scientists have finally found evidence of a particle decay so rare that it happens only once in roughly 10 billion decays, ending a search spanning more than 40 years. The breakthrough could help physicists uncover hidden particles and forces that lie beyond the reach of today's most powerful accelerators. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Gatineau Park foliage reveals local Cold War nuclear testing legacy
item.description: For more than six decades, local scientists have collected sugar maple leaves from Gatineau Park to measure their radiocarbon levels, creating the longest continuous record of its kind. Now, a study of those leaves led by the André E. Lalonde National Facility for Accelerator Mass Spectrometry (AEL-AMS) located at the University of Ottawa shows that the effects of Cold War–era nuclear weapons testing have only recently disappeared from the local biosphere. The study, titled "Stored carbohydrates buffer Bomb and Suess radiocarbon effects in maple leaves across a 65-year Ottawa region record,"… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Accidental discovery enables room-temperature recrystallization of molybdenum
item.description: Researchers at the University of Rochester and Technion–Israel Institute of Technology accidentally discovered a new way to rearrange the internal structure of molybdenum—an extremely heat-resistant metal—at room temperature. Molybdenum is typically used to reinforce nuclear reactors, jet engine turbine blades and rocket nozzles because it doesn't melt until it is heated to more than 2,600°C (4,712°F). Controlling its atomic structure at room temperature could open the door to more applications, including next-generation semiconductors. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study identifies single amino acid change that alters Andes virus protein behavior in human cells
item.description: Mount Sinai researchers have identified a single amino acid difference between rodent- and human-derived Andes virus isolates that changes how a key viral protein behaves inside human cells. The findings help explain biological differences between closely related virus isolates. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Starling numbers are declining—we're investigating whether their spectacular murmuration displays are changing too
item.description: Every autumn, from city centers to wetlands, starling murmurations attract crowds of spectators. Thousands of birds fill the sky, twisting and turning in extraordinary waves as the sun sets. An entire flock moves as one, creating shapes that shift and dissolve as quickly as they appear. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Methane-eating microbes grown on electrodes build electrically conductive nanowires
item.description: Certain microorganisms (anaerobic methanotrophic archaea, or ANME) consume methane and convert it into electricity, as research conducted four years ago by microbiologist Cornelia Welte of Radboud University revealed. New research by Welte and her colleagues published in Nature Communications now shows that these methane-consuming organisms do this by producing nanowires through which they can transmit the electricity they generate. The researchers have also succeeded in cultivating these specific microorganisms in almost pure form in the lab. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cracking the case of the Roman frog graveyard
item.description: Ten years after 8,000 ancient frog bones were discovered in a single ditch, scientists at Bournemouth University and the Museum of London Archaeology (MOLA) have finally identified the culprits Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Anglo-Saxon kingdom chose copper coins despite abundant silver
item.description: Analysis of silver and gold from the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Northumbria finds that, contrary to popular belief, it did not suffer from a shortage of precious metals, questioning why the kingdom used copper-alloy coins rather than silver like its contemporaries. Fuente: Phys.org.
